## LU-Factorization Background

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Definition - LU Factorization
A nonsingular matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ has an LU factorization if
$$
A = LU,
$$
where $L$ is lower triangular and $U$ is upper triangular.
:::

An LU factorization, when it exists, is not unique: for any nonsingular diagonal matrix $\Lambda$, $A=(L\Lambda)(\Lambda^{-1}U)$ is another one. Common normalizations fix the choice:

- Doolittle form: diagonal entries of $L$ are all $1$.
- Crout form: diagonal entries of $U$ are all $1$.
- Cholesky form (for symmetric positive definite $A$): $A=R^\top R$, where $R$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal entries (so $L=R^\top$ and $U=R$).

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Theorem - Solve via Factorization
If $A=LU$ with $A$ nonsingular (so every diagonal entry of $L$ and of $U$ is nonzero), then solving $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is equivalent to
$$
L\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b},\qquad U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}.
$$
So one forward substitution and one back substitution solve the original system.
:::

## Formulas

With $L_D,U_D$ the Doolittle factors, $L_C,U_C$ the Crout factors and $R$ the Cholesky factor, the three forms are:

$$
A=L_DU_D \quad \text{(Doolittle)},
\tag{1}
$$

$$
A=L_CU_C \quad \text{(Crout)},
\tag{2}
$$

$$
A=R^\top R \quad \text{(Cholesky, SPD matrices)}.
\tag{3}
$$

Matching the entries of $A$ with those of the product builds each factor one row or column at a time. Write $l_{ij},u_{ij},r_{ij}$ for the entries of the factor being computed; for $k=1,\dots,n$ (an empty sum is $0$):

**Doolittle** (row $k$ of $U$, then column $k$ of $L$; $l_{kk}=1$):
$$
u_{kj}=a_{kj}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}l_{ks}u_{sj}\quad(j=k,\dots,n),\qquad
l_{ik}=\frac{1}{u_{kk}}\Bigl(a_{ik}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}l_{is}u_{sk}\Bigr)\quad(i=k+1,\dots,n).
$$

**Crout** (column $k$ of $L$, then row $k$ of $U$; $u_{kk}=1$):
$$
l_{ik}=a_{ik}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}l_{is}u_{sk}\quad(i=k,\dots,n),\qquad
u_{kj}=\frac{1}{l_{kk}}\Bigl(a_{kj}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}l_{ks}u_{sj}\Bigr)\quad(j=k+1,\dots,n).
$$

**Cholesky** (row $k$ of $R$):
$$
r_{kk}=\sqrt{a_{kk}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}r_{sk}^2},\qquad
r_{kj}=\frac{1}{r_{kk}}\Bigl(a_{kj}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}r_{sk}r_{sj}\Bigr)\quad(j=k+1,\dots,n).
$$

Without pivoting, these recurrences succeed only while every divisor $u_{kk}$, $l_{kk}$ or $r_{kk}$ is nonzero (and, for Cholesky, every quantity under the square root is positive).

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Theorem - Cholesky Factorization
If $A$ is real, symmetric and positive definite, then it has a Cholesky factorization $A=R^\top R$ with $R$ upper triangular and $r_{kk}>0$; every quantity under the square root in the recurrence above is positive.
:::

## Example 1 - One Matrix, Three Factorizations

Factorize

$$
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&1&1&3&2\\
1&2&2&1&1\\
1&2&9&1&5\\
3&1&1&7&1\\
2&1&5&1&8
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

### Doolittle ($\operatorname{diag}(L_D)=1$)

$$
L_D=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&0&0\\
\tfrac12&1&0&0&0\\
\tfrac12&1&1&0&0\\
\tfrac32&-\tfrac13&0&1&0\\
1&0&\tfrac47&-\tfrac67&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U_D=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&1&1&3&2\\
0&\tfrac32&\tfrac32&-\tfrac12&0\\
0&0&7&0&4\\
0&0&0&\tfrac73&-2\\
0&0&0&0&2
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

### Crout ($\operatorname{diag}(U_C)=1$)

$$
L_C=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&0&0&0&0\\
1&\tfrac32&0&0&0\\
1&\tfrac32&7&0&0\\
3&-\tfrac12&0&\tfrac73&0\\
2&0&4&-2&2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U_C=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\tfrac12&\tfrac12&\tfrac32&1\\
0&1&1&-\tfrac13&0\\
0&0&1&0&\tfrac47\\
0&0&0&1&-\tfrac67\\
0&0&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

### Cholesky ($A=R^\top R$)

One valid upper-triangular Cholesky factor is

$$
R=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt2&\tfrac1{\sqrt2}&\tfrac1{\sqrt2}&\tfrac3{\sqrt2}&\sqrt2\\
0&\sqrt{\tfrac32}&\sqrt{\tfrac32}&-\tfrac1{\sqrt6}&0\\
0&0&\sqrt7&0&\tfrac4{\sqrt7}\\
0&0&0&\sqrt{\tfrac73}&-2\sqrt{\tfrac37}\\
0&0&0&0&\sqrt2
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Verification:**
$$
L_DU_D=A,\qquad L_CU_C=A,\qquad R^\top R=A.
$$

The Crout factors are the Doolittle factors rescaled by the pivots: $L_C=L_D\operatorname{diag}(U_D)$ with $\operatorname{diag}(U_D)=\operatorname{diag}(2,\tfrac32,7,\tfrac73,2)$, an instance of the non-uniqueness noted above.

## Example 2 - Solve $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ by Doolittle, Crout and Cholesky

Use the same $A$ and

$$
\mathbf{b}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-2\\4\\3\\-5\\1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

### (a) Doolittle

**Step 1:** Solve $L_D\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b}$.

$$
\mathbf{y}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-2\\5\\-1\\-\tfrac13\\\tfrac{23}{7}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2:** Solve $U_D\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}$.

$$
\mathbf{x}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-\tfrac{629}{98}\\[2pt]
\tfrac{237}{49}\\[2pt]
-\tfrac{53}{49}\\[2pt]
\tfrac{62}{49}\\[2pt]
\tfrac{23}{14}
\end{pmatrix}
\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
-6.41837\\4.83673\\-1.08163\\1.26531\\1.64286
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

### (b) Crout

**Step 1:** Solve $L_C\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b}$ by forward substitution.

$$
\mathbf{y}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-1\\\tfrac{10}{3}\\-\tfrac17\\-\tfrac17\\\tfrac{23}{14}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

This is the Doolittle $\mathbf{y}$ divided entrywise by the pivots $2,\tfrac32,7,\tfrac73,2$.

**Step 2:** Solve $U_C\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}$ by back substitution. It returns the same $\mathbf{x}$ as in part (a).

### (c) Cholesky

**Step 1:** Solve $R^\top\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b}$ by forward substitution.

$$
\mathbf{y}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-\sqrt2\\[2pt]\tfrac{5\sqrt6}{3}\\[2pt]-\tfrac{\sqrt7}{7}\\[2pt]-\tfrac{\sqrt{21}}{21}\\[2pt]\tfrac{23\sqrt2}{14}
\end{pmatrix}
\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
-1.41421\\4.08248\\-0.37796\\-0.21822\\2.32335
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

This is the Doolittle $\mathbf{y}$ divided entrywise by the square roots of the pivots.

**Step 2:** Solve $R\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}$ by back substitution. It again returns the same $\mathbf{x}$ as in part (a).

**Verification (all three parts):** parts (a), (b) and (c) give the same $\mathbf{x}$, and substituting it into $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ checks every row.

| Row | Left-hand side $A\mathbf{x}$ | Right-hand side |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $2x_1+x_2+x_3+3x_4+2x_5=-2$ | $-2\;\checkmark$ |
| 2 | $x_1+2x_2+2x_3+x_4+x_5=4$ | $4\;\checkmark$ |
| 3 | $x_1+2x_2+9x_3+x_4+5x_5=3$ | $3\;\checkmark$ |
| 4 | $3x_1+x_2+x_3+7x_4+x_5=-5$ | $-5\;\checkmark$ |
| 5 | $2x_1+x_2+5x_3+x_4+8x_5=1$ | $1\;\checkmark$ |

Mathews' module goes on to two applications of the Cholesky factorization that are not reproduced here: a least-squares cubic fitted to the six data points $(0,12)$, $(1,3)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,7)$, $(4,9)$, $(5,2)$ by solving the normal equations (his Example 3), and the continuous least-squares polynomial of degree 4 for $\cos x$ on $[0,1]$, whose Gram matrix is the $5\times5$ Hilbert matrix (his Example 4).
